blocks.p: The Hierarch of the Church of Life received him on his knees in a bean row, with dirt to the wrists.

The wardens brought Sol to the garden at the third hour of the morning. It lay in the innermost court of Sion, inside a wall of old white stone, and beyond the wall, very close, rose the great blind flank of the sanctum, windowless and white, going up and up until its top was lost in the bright haze. Inside the wall there were vegetables: beans on their poles, squash sprawling under broad leaves, onions, lettuces in careful rows, a fig tree against the warm stone. It smelled of turned earth and wet leaves and, faintly, of manure. It was the only place he had seen in Sion that smelled of anything.

The Hierarch was halfway down the bean row with a trowel. He was a small man, slight and narrow-shouldered, in a plain white smock gone brown at the knees, and when he heard them on the path he sat back on his heels and turned, and Sol saw his face.

He had forgotten it. He must have seen it a thousand times across a thousand tables, but thirty-two years away had worn it down, and now it came back all at once. A mild round face, almost childlike, renewed at about thirty-five. Close-cropped dark hair. And the eyes: large and grey and a little dazzled, always, like the eyes of a man who has just come in out of snow. They were the eyes that had looked on the Face of Light more often than any eyes alive, and they looked at Sol now, at his white head and his stoop, with no flinching in them at all. Only a vast, gentle, burning curiosity.
“Tarren,” the Hierarch said. “Oh. Look at you.”
He got up, without using his hands, the way the young get up, and came along the row and stopped in front of Sol, and wiped his palms on his smock.
“May I?” he said.

Sol did not know what he was asking. Then the Hierarch lifted one earthy hand and laid it, very lightly, against Sol’s cheek, and moved his thumb along the deep line that ran from the nose to the corner of the mouth, as a man might trace a crack in an old wall to see how far it went.

“So this is what it does,” he said softly. “I’ve seen it in the archival images. I never thought to see it on a friend.” He took his hand away and looked at the soil it had left on Sol’s face, and laughed, apologetic, and brushed it off. “Forgive me. Sit down. Your knees, I expect. Do they hurt?”
“Most days.”
“Every day?”
“Most days,” Sol said again.

There was a bench under the fig tree. The Hierarch sat at one end and Sol lowered himself onto the other, and the wardens withdrew to the gate, out of hearing, and stood there in their white with their hands folded.

“You won’t remember,” the Hierarch said, “but you held the Book of Life for me at my consecration. Two hundred and seventy years ago, in the old hall, before this one was built. My hands were shaking so badly I couldn’t hold it myself, and you saw, and you took it from me without a word and held it open for me to read, and your hands were perfectly steady.” He smiled. “I’ve always remembered that. I asked him once to let me keep it, and he did.”
“I don’t remember,” Sol said. “I’m sorry.”
“No. Of course not. You were renewed many times since.” The grey eyes went over him again, unhurried. “And now never again. That’s the part I can’t take in. You’ll go on like this. Further.”
“Until I stop.”

“Until you stop.” The Hierarch said it carefully, as if it were a word in a language he was learning. “Tell me. I’m not asking as the Consistory asks; they’ll do that tomorrow, and badly. I’m asking for myself. Who took you into the water?”
“A friend,” Sol said. “You won’t get his name from me, Hierarch. Not even you.”
The Hierarch nodded, as though that were the answer he had expected and in some way the answer he had wanted. “And how many have you taken in yourself?”
“Four hundred and twelve.”
“You know the number.”

“I know their names. I used to count the forms. I found I couldn’t stop counting.” Sol looked at his hands. “Four hundred and twelve people who can’t be renewed now, or ascended. Who will get old, and die.”
“And you sleep at night?”
“Not always.”

A bird had come down into the bean row, a small brown sparrow-thing, and was working at the turned earth. They watched it a while. Somewhere beyond the garden wall a bell rang once, and the sound came back off the white flank of the sanctum.

“I read the releases,” the Hierarch said. “Did you know that? Every one that comes up from Serenity, and from all the other houses, for two hundred years. I read every name. I sign some of them myself, when the bishop who took custody can’t be found.” His voice was entirely gentle. “They go to rest, Tarren. The noise is taken out of them, and the pattern is released, and there is no one left anywhere who can suffer, or be afraid. I’ve thought about it a great deal. It’s the kindest thing we do.”

“I watched one,” Sol said. “Stephen Hale. On Serenity, in a white room, with flowers in it. They couldn’t use his Halo; it was dark, like mine. So they used a needle. He lay down on the bed and he wasn’t afraid, and he wasn’t confused, and there was no noise in him anywhere. He was saying a psalm. He was looking up at something I couldn’t see, and he said, It’s open. And then he prayed for me. For me, Hierarch. I had my name on the form in the corner of my eye, and he asked his god not to hold it against me.” His voice had begun to go, and he let it. “Then he stopped breathing. That’s what we do. That’s all it is. I signed for thousands.”

The Hierarch did not look away. That was the strangest thing; Sol had told this to wardens and bishops and colonists, and they all looked away, or covered their ears, or went smooth. The Hierarch listened to every word with his dazzled eyes on Sol’s face.
“You believe that,” he said at last.
“I saw it.”
“Yes. I can see that you did.” He turned the trowel over in his hands. “And the voice? On the packet, after? They say you heard a voice.”
“I did.”
“What did it say?”
“It asked me why I was hunting him.” Sol looked up at the fig leaves. “I didn’t know I was. I thought I was helping. I thought I was the kindest man in the church.”
“You were,” the Hierarch said simply. “Everyone said so.”
“Then the church should be very frightened of its kind men.”
The Hierarch smiled at that, a small rueful smile, the smile of a man at his own table hearing a guest say something outrageous that he secretly enjoys. Then it faded.

“Tell me about him,” he said. “The one whose name you say. No,” he put up a hand, quickly, “don’t say it. Please. Not here, not in my garden. If you say it in the Consistory tomorrow, I’ll have to hear it there, and I’d rather not hear it twice.” He looked down at his earthy hands. “And don’t tell me all of it. I read the releases; I know what you’ll have told the others. Tell me one thing he did. Only one. The way you’d tell me about a plant I’d never seen grow.”

Sol thought about it. He had told it whole so many times, in lofts and granaries and seed houses, the well and the boy and the careful men in good robes, that it had worn a groove in him. He looked at the bean poles and the turned earth and the small man in the brown-kneed smock, and told him something else.

“They buried him in a garden,” he said. “There was a garden by the place where they killed him, and a new tomb cut in the rock, and they put him there because it was close and the light was going. And early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, a woman came to the garden to do the last thing for him that anyone could do. The stone was rolled away. He was gone.” Sol’s hands lay open on his knees. “She stood outside the tomb and wept. She didn’t know what else to do. And a man came up behind her in the half dark, and she took him for the gardener. That’s in the book, Hierarch. And the first thing he said to her was, Woman, why are you weeping?”
The trowel had stopped turning in the Hierarch’s hands.

“He asked her,” Sol said. “He was standing there alive, with the whole answer in his own body, and he asked her what was wrong, and waited while she told him. She said, If you’ve carried him away, tell me where you’ve laid him. And he said her name. Only that. And she knew him.” He looked at the soil under the Hierarch’s nails. “Your god wipes the tears away before anyone has cried them. Mine let a woman finish crying in a garden, and then called her by her name. That’s the whole of the difference between them. That’s all I came to say.”
The Hierarch sat very still. The sparrow had gone.

“I go in to him every evening,” he said, after a long time. “At the last office. Did you know? Every evening for two hundred and seventy years, except when I was being renewed, and once when I had a fever.” He was looking at the white flank of the sanctum over the wall, and his face had changed: it had opened, and gone young, and the dazzle in his eyes had deepened until it was almost painful to see. “The doors open. I walk out onto the sea of glass, and it holds me up, and the light moves down in it like fish. And the saints are there on their thrones all around, the first holy ones, with their hands folded. And the rainbow. You remember the rainbow. Green. So green the eye can’t find the end of it. And then I lift my head and he’s there.”
He breathed in.

“When I was young,” he said, “it was my mother’s face. I don’t remember her at all, otherwise. Only there. Then for a long time it was faces I’d loved and lost track of. Lately it isn’t anyone’s. It’s simply his own. It’s simply the face of someone who has been waiting all day for me to come in, and is glad I came. Every day, Tarren. For two hundred and seventy years. Can you understand that? I have never once gone in there and found him tired of me.”

Sol could understand it. He had stood there eleven times. He remembered the light that was not like light, and his knees going out from under him, and the face he had known all his life and could not name. He remembered coming out with the feeling that he would never need anything again. He tried to think what he would see now, with his Halo dark, and could not imagine it at all.
“They say you come out weeping,” he said. “Without tears.”
The Hierarch’s hand went, without his seeming to know it, to his own throat.

“It’s true,” he said. “Something rises. Every time. It comes up from somewhere very low and gets as far as here,” his fingers moved against his throat, “and stops. I don’t know what it is. I asked him once to let me finish it. Whatever it was. He said there was no need; that there are no tears in the new creation, and he had wiped them all away. He was right, of course.” He let his hand fall. “Is it true that you weep? They say you wept on Philippa, at funerals, in front of children.”
“Yes.”
“What is it like?”

Sol thought about it. “Like a fever breaking,” he said. “Like putting down something heavy you didn’t know you’d been carrying for hours, and finding your arms are shaking. And then you have to pick it up again. And you find you’re glad to. Because it’s yours, and it was someone you loved.”
The Hierarch looked at him for a long moment. Something moved behind the grey eyes, deep down, the way a fish moves under a bright surface, and Sol could not tell what it was.
“Bishop Croft has asked for a full curation,” the Hierarch said. “At the autumn renewal. Did he tell you? I signed it this morning. It seemed the kind thing.”
“Don’t let them do it.”
“He’s suffering, Tarren. We don’t let people suffer.”

“It’s the only door he has left. The suffering. If you take it out of him, there’s no way back to anything. He’ll be smooth and fond and amused for the rest of time, and he’ll never once know what he lost.” Sol put his hand on the bench between them. “I’m asking you. As the man who held the book. Unsign it.”
The Hierarch looked down at Sol’s hand, at the brown spots and the tremor in it. He did not take it. But he did not move away from it either.
“I’ll think about it,” he said quietly. “I can promise you that. I’ll think about it.”

He was quiet a while. Then he said, in a different voice, the voice of the Hierarch rather than the gardener: “Will you go under the hood for me? Tonight? Sometimes a dark Halo comes back. It happens out in the colonies all the time. We could try.”
“Not mine,” Sol said.

“Then say the words for me. Only once. I’ll take that to the Consistory, and it will help you more than you know.” He leaned forward, and his face was pleading, and entirely sincere. “Remember the Mountain.”
Sol was silent for a long moment. The bell beyond the wall rang again, twice, for the fourth hour.
“I remember the Mountain,” he said. “I’ll remember it as long as I live, Hierarch. I won’t forget the tears.”

The Hierarch closed his eyes. When he opened them, the pleading had gone out of his face, and what was left was only sorrow, the dry, puzzled sorrow of a man who does not know the name of what he feels.

“Then they’ll ask me to release you,” he said. “Tomorrow. You know that. The Advocate will ask, and the bench will agree, and I’ll have to say yes.” He looked at the sanctum wall. “But I’d like you to see him again first. Before. I’d like you to stand in front of him one more time, with me beside you. Not as a sentence. As a friend. Eleven times you stood there, Tarren, and came out whole. I have never known anyone stand there and not be healed of whatever was wrong with him.” He turned back. “Will you come? If I ask it?”
Sol thought of Stephen on the cot in the white room, lying back slowly like an old man in an archival image. I’m not afraid. I’d like you not to be.
“I’ll go wherever you take me,” he said.

The Hierarch smiled at him then, with his whole face, the way the ascended smiled, and the way, Sol suddenly remembered, the young man with the shaking hands had smiled at him over the open Book of Life two hundred and seventy years ago. He got up and called the wardens with a small lift of his hand.

At the edge of the garden there was a tap set into the wall. The Hierarch went to it and washed his hands under it, carefully, rubbing at the earth in the creases of his knuckles, while the wardens came to help Sol up. The water ran brown and then clear.

“I go in at noon as well, before a Consistory,” he said, shaking his hands dry. “I like to ask him about the day.” He hesitated, and looked at Sol over his shoulder with his dazzled eyes, and his face was kind. “Shall I ask him anything for you?”
Sol stood between the two wardens with the smell of the turned earth all around him.
“Ask him why he won’t let you finish weeping,” he said.
The Hierarch went very still by the tap. For a breath, perhaps two, something rose in his face, came up from somewhere very low, and got as far as his eyes.
Then it stopped. He smiled.
“I know why,” he said gently. “There’s no need.”

He went away along the colonnade toward the inner court, a small man in a white smock with the brown still on its knees, walking quickly, the way a man walks toward someone he loves. Sol watched him until the white stone hid him. There was still a line of dirt under his fingernails; Sol had seen it when he raised his hand to the wardens.
He was the happiest man Sol had ever met. And Sol had never been so sorry for anyone.
